transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Hi there, please share your thoughts on what democracy means to you personally?.

transcript.speaker: respondent
transcript.text: Well, I've lived through some pretty tumultuous times where everyone seems to want to shake things up, but I tend to lean towards the idea of stability and order. Democracy often feels like it's in a constant state of debate, which can be a bit disorienting at times for someone who just wants things to be as they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Stability and order often seem important, especially in turbulent times. Could you give an example of what might feel disruptive to your sense of stability and order?

transcript.speaker: respondent
transcript.text: Sure, things like sudden changes or instability in government, or too much debate without resolution can feel very disruptive. I like things to be predictable and work more or less the same way they've always been. Things changing too much or unpredictably can throw me off for sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Things changing unpredictably can be quite disruptive. Can you think of a specific time when something felt very unpredictable and disruptive to you?

transcript.speaker: respondent
transcript.text: Well, I remember during the big financial crisis. The markets weren’t stable; there were these big shifts and uncertainty in everything, and people were making decisions that seemed really uncertain and uncontrolled. That really threw me off a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: During the financial crisis, things felt very unpredictable. Could you describe how the uncertainty affected you personally?

transcript.speaker: respondent
transcript.text: Sure, during the financial crisis, everything felt very uncertain. The markets were going up and down quickly, and people were making big decisions without much clarity. It made me feel a bit uneasy. I prefer things that have some stability and that people know what to expect. Those unpredictable swings just seemed to unsettle me a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Uncertainty really did unsettle you during the financial crisis. Can you give me an example of a decision that seemed uncertain to you during that time?

transcript.speaker: respondent
transcript.text: During the financial crisis, one thing that really felt uncertain was the decisions companies were making. There were a lot of layoffs, but nobody knew exactly how long things were going to be like. There was this big uncertainty about the future, and it was hard to plan. I felt like I didn’t have a clear idea of what to expect for the next month or the next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Uncertainty about future decisions definitely threw you off. Can you share a specific example of a situation where you were not sure what to expect next?

transcript.speaker: respondent
transcript.text: During the financial crisis, there were days when I thought the markets might crash again, and I wasn’t sure when things would stabilize. It was hard to plan my finances because I didn’t know when the economy would improve or if it would improve at all. That kind of uncertainty definitely threw me off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Uncertainty about the future certainly can be unsettling. Can you think of any plans or expectations that were affected by the uncertainty?

transcript.speaker: respondent
transcript.text: Sure, during the financial crisis, I had to re-evaluate a lot of my plans and expectations. I tried to reduce my debts, but I didn’t know if that was the right move because the future was so uncertain. Planning for retirement felt different too, not knowing when I might have a steady income. So many things changed expectations and plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your plans and expectations were disrupted by the uncertainty during the financial crisis. Can you explain how a specific plan was affected?

transcript.speaker: respondent
transcript.text: Oh, definitely. One plan that was affected was saving for retirement. I had to think about cutting back a bit because I wasn’t sure about job security or the market. If something changed, I’d need to be prepared, so I tried to reduce some debts and cut back on other things to make savings easier. It made planning more uncertain too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Reducing debts and cutting back on spending became more uncertain with the financial crisis. Can you describe how this change in your plan for retirement affected you?

transcript.speaker: respondent
transcript.text: Absolutely. When the financial crisis hit, I knew I had to be more careful with my finances. So, I started cutting back on spending a bit. I figured if the economy was uncertain, I wouldn’t want to make big commitments like saving for retirement because I didn’t know if I would be able to stick to the plan. It made everything a bit more uncertain, and I felt like I needed to be cautious in my financial planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Being cautious in your financial planning made your retirement savings feel uncertain. Can you elaborate on how this made your financial goals less certain?

transcript.speaker: respondent
transcript.text: Sure. With the financial crisis, I had to be very careful with my money. I didn’t want to put too much into savings because I wasn’t sure the market would be stable or if I would be able to keep up with my retirement plan. So, my goal of having a certain amount saved for retirement became really uncertain. I had to be more flexible with my plans to make sure I wouldn’t run out of money. It made everything feel a bit more precarious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Being careful with your money made your retirement savings feel more uncertain. Can you share more about how you adjusted your plans to be more flexible?

transcript.speaker: respondent
transcript.text: You see, I started cutting back on some non-essential spending and tried to find ways to save a bit more from what I had. I also looked into more flexible investment options, maybe things that were a bit safer during the uncertain times. I wanted to keep some cushion in case things didn’t go as planned. It made my plans more flexible, but also made them feel a bit less certain too. But I knew I had to be prepared, so I tried my best to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Adjusting your plans to be more flexible made your retirement savings feel uncertain. Can you tell me more about the more flexible investment options you considered?

transcript.speaker: respondent
transcript.text: Sure, I looked into some more conservative investment options like bonds and stable investment accounts. I heard they were a bit safer during uncertain times, so I tried to include more of those in my portfolio. I also looked into monthly investment plans, where I would invest a fixed amount every month rather than trying to save a lump sum. This way, if the market wasn’t as good for a while, I could still keep things going. It was more about finding ways to be a bit more resilient and less risky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you for sharing your thoughts with me. It's been informative.

transcript.speaker: respondent
transcript.text: You're welcome! It was good talking with you. If you have any more questions or if there’s anything else I can share, feel free to ask.
